analysis.one_liner: Bans companies from using surveillance data to charge different shoppers different prices for the same thing.
analysis.headline: The One Fair Price Act was introduced in the Senate on December 8, 2025 and referred to the Commerce Committee, with 4 of 45 Senate Democrats cosponsoring; no further action has been taken [S4].
analysis.plain_summary: Companies increasingly use personal data—browsing history, location, device type—to decide what price to show each shopper, a practice often called surveillance pricing. This bill would make it illegal to charge different people different prices for the same or substantially similar product based on that data. It keeps normal discounts (senior, military, teacher, loyalty programs) legal, and it lets the Federal Trade Commission, state attorneys general, and individual consumers enforce the rule, with penalties starting at $3,000 per violation.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyday consumers who shop online or use apps, especially people whose data suggests they can be charged more—frequent buyers, loyal customers, people in pricier neighborhoods, or anyone whose device type or browsing history marks them as less price-sensitive. The bill also gives individuals a new way to sue, even voiding pre-dispute arbitration agreements and class-action waivers for these claims.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits offering or charging different prices to different consumers for the same or a substantially similar product when informed by surveillance data—personal information, behavior, or biometrics [S2].

Preserves ordinary discounts—teachers, military, veterans, seniors, students, and knowingly enrolled loyalty programs—as long as eligibility rules are clearly disclosed and loyalty data isn't reused for profiling or individualized pricing [S2].

Gives consumers a private right of action with a minimum $3,000 recovery per violation, triple damages for willful violations, attorney's fees, and a rule making pre-dispute arbitration agreements and class-action waivers unenforceable for these claims [S2].
Adds air carriers, foreign air carriers, and ticket agents explicitly, and clarifies that federal aviation law does not preempt these claims or block state attorneys general [S2].
Lets the FTC enforce against not just ordinary companies but also common carriers, nonprofits, and airlines, which normal FTC jurisdiction does not reach [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Retailers, e-commerce platforms, airlines, ticket sellers, and any business that uses customer data to individualize prices would have to abandon that practice and could face lawsuits with $3,000-per-violation minimums and easy-to-meet burden-shifting rules. Data brokers and ad-tech firms lose a market for selling data used to set prices. Insurance and credit products are exempt [S2].

drawbacks.text: Cost-based price differences are only allowed if disclosed to the consumer before purchase, which would force companies to explain logistics-related pricing variations—and arguably ban some legitimate price variation that benefits shoppers [S2].

The presumption that a seller is violating the law whenever two shoppers see different prices for the same product puts the burden on businesses to prove innocence, and small businesses without compliance departments could face real exposure, which is why the bill requires a Regulatory Flexibility Act review and an SBA small-business impact study [S2].
Defining what counts as the same or a substantially similar product, and tracing whether a price was partly informed by data, could generate years of litigation over ambiguous cases [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core protection—no charging individuals more because of what your data says about them—addresses a practice most shoppers find unfair and that is hard to detect without a law like this. The main cost is compliance and litigation risk, especially for small sellers, and the presumption-of-violation structure is aggressive. The bill excludes insurance and credit, so the sectors where risk-based pricing is most entrenched are untouched. On balance it is a meaningful consumer protection with a blunt enforcement design.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee on the same day in December 2025, and has not moved since.

narrative.text: Sen. Ruben Gallego introduced S. 3387, the One Fair Price Act of 2025, on December 8, 2025 [S1].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation; that referral is the only action on record [S2,S4].
Four of 45 Senate Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans have [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No outcome yet—companies using surveillance pricing continue under current law while the bill sits in committee.

for.name: Sen. Ruben Gallego
for.role: U.S. Senator from Arizona; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the One Fair Price Act and referred it to the Senate Commerce Committee.

sides.party_line_note: Only Democrats have sponsored or cosponsored so far; no Republican has signed on and no vote has occurred, so the partisan shape of a floor fight is unknown.

industries.note: The bill bans using purchased surveillance data to set individualized prices, removing a market for behavioral data tied to pricing. Their business depends on charging through data consumers never knowingly sold.

They would have to stop testing different prices on different shoppers, ending a tool for extracting the maximum each customer will pay; consumers keep more of their surplus. Loyalty discounts remain legal if disclosed.

Section 3 expressly applies the ban to air carriers, foreign air carriers, and ticket agents and ensures these claims are not preempted, closing a gap left when the Senate stalled an FAA-related provision on surveillance pricing. Ticket prices informed by passenger data would be off-limits.
The bill expressly exempts the business of insurance and credit products, leaving risk-based pricing built on personal data untouched in the sectors where it is most pervasive.

analysis.trajectory: Roughly 90% of Senate bills die in committee, and this one has just one committee referral, four cosponsors, and no Republican support in a 55-55 Republican-controlled Senate; it is unlikely to get floor time in this Congress unless it attaches to a larger moving vehicle.
